summary: Securus Technologies, a US telecom company, has trained AI models on years of prison phone calls and is piloting them to monitor inmate communications in real time to predict and prevent crimes. The company has lobbied successfully to allow the costs of these AI surveillance tools to be passed on to inmates and their families, reversing a 2024 FCC reform. Critics argue this is coercive consent and invasive surveillance that outpaces the law.

claims.text: Securus Technologies trained an AI model on seven years of calls made by inmates in the Texas prison system.
claims.evidence_quote: It created one model, for example, using seven years of calls made by inmates in the Texas prison system

claims.text: Securus has been piloting AI tools to monitor inmate conversations in real time over the past year.
claims.evidence_quote: Over the past year, Elder says, Securus has been piloting the AI tools to monitor inmate conversations in real time.

claims.text: The AI model flags sections of conversations for human agents to review, who then send them to investigators.
claims.evidence_quote: The model will analyze phone and video calls, text messages, and emails and then flag sections for human agents to review. These agents then send them to investigators for follow-up.

claims.text: Securus claims its monitoring efforts have helped disrupt human trafficking and gang activities organized from within prisons.
claims.evidence_quote: Elder said Securus’ monitoring efforts have helped disrupt human trafficking and gang activities organized from within prisons

claims.text: Securus did not provide MIT Technology Review with any cases specifically uncovered by its new AI models.
claims.evidence_quote: But the company did not provide MIT Technology Review with any cases specifically uncovered by its new AI models.

claims.text: Inmates and their contacts are notified that conversations are recorded, but not that they may be used to train AI.
claims.evidence_quote: People in prison, and those they call, are notified that their conversations are recorded. But this doesn’t mean they’re aware that those conversations could be used to train an AI model

claims.text: Bianca Tylek called the consent for using inmate data 'coercive consent' because inmates have no other way to communicate with family.
claims.evidence_quote: “That’s coercive consent; there’s literally no other way you can communicate with your family,” Tylek says.

claims.text: Inmates in most states pay for calls, so they are charged while their data is collected for AI training.
claims.evidence_quote: since inmates in the vast majority of states pay for these calls, she adds, “not only are you not compensating them for the use of their data, but you’re actually charging them while collecting their data.”

claims.text: Securus has a history of improperly recording calls between inmates and their attorneys.
claims.evidence_quote: leaks of its recordings databases showed the company had improperly recorded thousands of calls between inmates and their attorneys.

claims.text: Corene Kendrick said the AI system enables invasive surveillance and courts have specified few limits.
claims.evidence_quote: “I think this is one of many situations where the technology is way far ahead of the law.”

claims.text: In 2024, the FCC issued a reform forbidding telecoms from passing the costs of recording and surveilling calls on to inmates.
claims.evidence_quote: In 2024, the Federal Communications Commission issued a major reform... that forbade telecoms from passing the costs of recording and surveilling calls on to inmates.

claims.text: In June, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr postponed all deadlines for jails and prisons to adopt the 2024 reforms.
claims.evidence_quote: In June, Brendan Carr... said it would postpone all deadlines for jails and prisons to adopt the 2024 reforms

claims.text: On October 28, the FCC voted to pass new, higher rate caps and allow companies to pass security costs, including AI tools, on to inmates.
claims.evidence_quote: On October 28, the agency went further: It voted to pass new, higher rate caps and allow companies like Securus to pass security costs relating to recording and monitoring of calls—like storing recordings, transcribing them, or building AI tools to analyze such calls, for example—on to inmates.

claims.text: FCC commissioner Anna Gomez dissented, saying law enforcement should foot the bill, not families of incarcerated people.
claims.evidence_quote: “Law enforcement,” she wrote in a statement, “should foot the bill for unrelated security and safety costs, not the families of incarcerated people.”
